title: A 28-Year-Old Crew Member Died Building a Set for Rajinikanth’s ‘Jailer 2’ — and Indian Cinema’s Safety Reckoning Is Long Overdue
excerpt: T. Karthikeyan was electrocuted while working on art direction at Chennai’s Adityaram Film City. Production has halted, police are investigating, and the industry is once again forced to confront what it does to protect the people behind the camera.
body:
T. Karthikeyan was twenty-eight years old, working in the art department, and doing what thousands of below-the-line crew members do on Indian film sets every day: building the world the audience will eventually see. On 14 May, while erecting a house-like structure on the set of *Jailer 2* at Chennai’s Adityaram Film City, he came into contact with a live electrical source. He died of electrocution.

Production on the Rajinikanth-starrer, directed by Nelson Dilipkumar, was immediately halted. Kanathur Police registered a case and launched an investigation into the electrical leak that killed Karthikeyan. The film, a sequel to the 2023 blockbuster that grossed over ₹600 crore worldwide, had been in active production with a tentative release date of June–September 2026.

## The details that matter

Karthikeyan was part of the art direction team — the crew responsible for constructing physical sets, painting backdrops, and dressing locations. It is physically demanding, often hazardous work that happens under tight deadlines, usually before the stars arrive on set. Electrical safety on Indian film sets is governed by a patchwork of local regulations and production-house internal policies, with no national standard equivalent to the UK’s Health and Safety at Work Act or the US OSHA regulations that govern American film productions.

According to initial police reports, the electrocution was caused by an electrical leakage — a failure that, in a properly inspected production environment, should have been caught by residual current devices or pre-shoot safety checks. Whether such checks were conducted is now a matter for the investigation.

## An industry pattern

Karthikeyan’s death is not an isolated incident. Indian film productions have a grim record of set accidents that rarely make national headlines unless a major star is involved. Stunt performers, lighting technicians, and construction crew face risks that are amplified by the speed at which Indian productions operate — shooting schedules are compressed, budgets for below-the-line safety equipment are thin, and the freelance nature of most crew employment means there is no institutional incentive to invest in long-term safety infrastructure.

The Federation of Western India Cine Employees (FWICE) and its southern counterparts have periodically called for mandatory safety audits on all active sets, accredited electrical supervisors for any production using more than basic power loads, comprehensive insurance coverage for all crew — not just principal cast — and incident reporting protocols with consequences for non-compliance. Progress on all four has been glacial.

## The Rajinikanth factor

The involvement of Rajinikanth — arguably the most bankable star in South Indian cinema — gives this tragedy a visibility that most set accidents do not receive. *Jailer* was a phenomenon: it earned ₹604 crore globally, performed strongly in NRI markets across North America, the UK, and the Gulf, and cemented Rajinikanth’s commercial relevance at seventy-five. The sequel carries enormous expectations and an equally enormous budget.

High-budget productions are, paradoxically, not always safer. The scale of construction, the number of crew on set, and the pressure to deliver on schedule can create conditions where corners are cut. Whether that happened on the *Jailer 2* set is for the police to determine, but the structural incentives are clear.

## What the diaspora should know

If you watched *Jailer* in a Cinemark in New Jersey or a Vue in London, you contributed to a ₹600-crore machine. That machine runs on the labour of people like Karthikeyan — young technicians who work gruelling hours for a fraction of what their American or British counterparts earn, often without the safety nets that Western unions have negotiated over decades.

The diaspora’s economic power in Indian cinema is real and growing. Overseas box-office receipts now account for fifteen to twenty per cent of a major Tamil or Hindi film’s total gross. That money comes with a kind of moral leverage that has barely been exercised. When NRI audiences demand subtitles, simultaneous global releases, and IMAX prints, the industry listens. Whether it would listen to demands for crew safety standards is an open question — but it is one worth asking.

## What comes next

The Kanathur Police investigation is ongoing. Adityaram Film City management has not issued a public statement. The *Jailer 2* production timeline is now uncertain, though industry sources expect filming to resume after the investigation concludes and safety measures are reviewed. Karthikeyan’s family has not spoken publicly.
